therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely exhausting — the pace in your voice and the weight in your words both tell me you're running on fumes, and that kind of sustained pressure is really hard on a person. You're right that therapy won't make the stress disappear, and I appreciate your honesty about that skepticism — but what we can work on together is shifting how you're relating to all of this, so it doesn't feel quite so relentless and out of control. Would it be okay if we started by just looking at what's driving that constant edge you're feeling, and whether some of the pressure you're under is coming from the situation itself or also from how you're thinking about it?

That's the part we can work with — not to deny reality, but to help your brain learn that it doesn't have to be scanning for danger every single moment, even when the circumstances genuinely are demanding.

That small shift from fighting your thoughts to redirecting your focus is often where people start to find some actual breathing room.

therapist: You just named something really sophisticated — the anxiety has built itself a closed loop where it takes credit for every good outcome, which makes it feel unfalsifiable and exhausting to challenge, and I can hear that exhaustion in how quickly and tensely you're working through this even right now. But here's the crack in that logic worth examining: if your vigilance were truly the only thing standing between you and disaster, you'd expect to see *some* correlation between your worry level and your actual performance — so on the days you've been most anxious, have you actually done your best work, or has the worry sometimes gotten in the way more than it's helped? That's not a rhetorical question — it's real evidence your brain can't as easily dismiss.

The goal isn't to prove you can handle high stakes without anxiety yet — it's just to show your nervous system, in tiny doses, that it's capable of easing off the accelerator without the wheels coming off.
